Explanation: These mature (high-adaptive) ego defenses manage uncomfortable impulses or emotions adaptively; suppression is deliberate postponement and sublimation channels impulses into constructive activity.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Adaptive ego defenses; High-adaptive defenses; Mature defenses
Source Section: Psychology / Mature Ego Defenses; PDF p. 9
Notes: All four are canonical high-adaptive defenses (Vaillant, Am Psychol 2000, PMID 11392869; Metzger, J Clin Psychol 2014). Board caution: anticipation, affiliation, self-assertion are also mature defenses and make strong decoys.

Explanation: Reinforcement increases behavior and punishment decreases it; positive means adding a stimulus and negative means removing one, forming the 2x2 operant contingency grid.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Four operant conditioning contingencies; Operant contingency grid
Source Section: Psychology / Operant Conditioning; PDF p. 4
Notes: Standard Skinnerian learning theory; these four are mutually exclusive and exhaustive. No primary trial reference needed or retrieved; foundational behavioral-science content.

Explanation: These four diagnoses constitute DSM-5-TR Cluster B, grouped by dramatic, emotional, or erratic traits.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Dramatic-emotional personality cluster; DSM Cluster B
Source Section: Personality Disorders / Cluster B; PDF p. 33
Notes: Exact DSM-5-TR Cluster B membership (American Psychiatric Association, DSM-5-TR, 2022). Clear and complete; no competing category.

Explanation: DSM-5 PTSD comprises four symptom clusters after qualifying trauma: intrusion/re-experiencing, avoidance, negative alterations in cognition and mood, and altered arousal/reactivity.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: PTSD symptom clusters; DSM-5 PTSD criteria B-E
Source Section: Anxiety, Trauma, and Stress Disorders / Trauma Disorders; PDF p. 28
Notes: Four-cluster model confirmed (Ressler et al., Nat Rev Neurol 2022; Williams et al., Cochrane 2026; Brewin et al., World Psychiatry 2025). Board overlap: acute stress disorder shares symptoms but is <1 month; ICD-11 uses a 3-cluster model.

Connection Title: Features of depression with atypical features
Explanation: Atypical-features specifier requires mood reactivity plus two or more of increased appetite/weight, hypersomnia, leaden paralysis, or rejection sensitivity; these four need not all be present.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Atypical depressive features; Reversed vegetative symptoms
Source Section: Psychotic and Mood Disorders / Depression Subtypes; PDF p. 38
Notes: Confirmed (APA DSM-5-TR 2022; Zahra et al., Clin Psychol Psychother 2025; Otte et al., Nat Rev Dis Primers 2016). Mood reactivity is the required gateway feature; interpersonal rejection sensitivity is a fifth feature and strong decoy. Not a complete diagnostic checklist.

Explanation: These positive symptoms reflect added disturbances of belief, perception, speech, or behavior and are not specific to schizophrenia.
Source Section: Psychotic and Mood Disorders / Schizophrenia; PDF p. 41
Notes: DSM-5 positive symptoms (Marder & Cannon, NEJM 2019). Board overlap: schizoaffective, brief psychotic, schizophreniform, and substance-induced psychosis share these; do not present as diagnostic of schizophrenia.

Explanation: Narcolepsy can combine excessive daytime sleepiness with REM-intrusion phenomena: cataplexy, sleep paralysis, and hypnagogic/hypnopompic hallucinations.
Source Section: Sleep and Psychosomatic Conditions / Sleep Disorders; PDF p. 50
Notes: Tetrad confirmed (Maski & Scammell, JAMA 2026; Sum-Ping & Mignot, JAMA 2023; Dauvilliers et al., Nat Rev Neurol 2014). Qualifier: cataplexy defines narcolepsy type 1 and is absent in type 2; the complete tetrad occurs in a minority.

Explanation: Recurrent self-induced vomiting can erode dental enamel, enlarge salivary (parotid) glands, produce knuckle calluses (Russell sign), and cause potassium loss with metabolic alkalosis.
Source Section: Anxiety, Trauma, and Stress Disorders / Eating Disorders; PDF p. 29
Notes: Confirmed (Attia & Walsh, JAMA 2025; APA DSM-5-TR 2022; Hornberger & Lane, AAP 2021). Findings reflect vomiting specifically (not all purging) and can also occur with vomiting in anorexia binge-purge subtype; calluses are not universal.

Explanation: Prolonged undernutrition in anorexia can produce fine lanugo hair, reproductive suppression (amenorrhea), reduced bone density, and nutrient deficits; these are complications, not mandatory criteria.
Source Section: Anxiety, Trauma, and Stress Disorders / Eating Disorders; PDF p. 29
Notes: Lanugo, amenorrhea, osteoporosis confirmed (Hornberger & Lane, AAP 2021). Board caution: 'Nutritional deficiencies' is a broad category rather than a discrete sign and overlaps other causes of severe undernutrition. Amenorrhea is no longer a required DSM-5 criterion.

Explanation: Opioid withdrawal commonly produces yawning and increased lacrimal, nasal, and gastrointestinal activity; the combination favors withdrawal over intoxication.
Source Section: Substance Misuse / Opioids; PDF p. 59
Notes: DSM-5 opioid withdrawal signs (APA DSM-5-TR 2022; Volkow & Blanco, Mol Psychiatry 2021; Gowing et al., Cochrane 2017). Selected set; each sign alone is nonspecific and not the complete syndrome.

Explanation: These selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors raise synaptic serotonin by inhibiting the serotonin transporter.
Source Section: Psychiatric Pharmacology / SSRIs; PDF p. 74
Notes: Class confirmed (AAP serotonin-syndrome table, Chun et al. 2016, lists citalopram/fluoxetine/sertraline as SSRIs). Board caution: escitalopram is the S-enantiomer of citalopram, so the pair are near-duplicates and could be contested as distinct tiles; keep them on separate boards if possible. Not an exhaustive class (paroxetine, fluvoxamine omitted).

Connection Title: SNRIs inhibiting serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake
Explanation: These serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors block both serotonin and norepinephrine transporters, with differing relative potencies across drugs and doses.
Source Section: Psychiatric Pharmacology / SNRIs; PDF p. 75
Notes: All four are SNRIs; levomilnacipran (Fetzima) is the most noradrenergic. Source PDF heading mislabels SNRI as 'selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor'; the correct expansion is serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (connection content is correct as written). Milnacipran omitted from the class list.

Explanation: These TCAs act via monoamine reuptake inhibition and have clinically important receptor-blocking (anticholinergic, antihistaminic, alpha-adrenergic) effects; relative serotonin vs norepinephrine effects differ.
Source Section: Psychiatric Pharmacology / Tricyclic Antidepressants; PDF p. 76
Notes: Class membership confirmed (AAP serotonin table lists amitriptyline, clomipramine, nortriptyline as TCAs; imipramine is prototypical). Do not convert source arrhythmia/sodium-bicarbonate wording into a dosing/treatment rule without independent review.

Connection Title: Benzodiazepines with oxidative phase I metabolism
Explanation: These benzodiazepines undergo oxidative (CYP450 phase I) metabolism before conjugation, distinguishing them from the lorazepam-oxazepam-temazepam group that is cleared by glucuronidation alone.
Source Section: Substance Misuse / Benzodiazepines; PDF p. 61
Notes: Confirmed: alprazolam/midazolam/diazepam/chlordiazepoxide are CYP3A4/2C19 substrates while lorazepam/oxazepam/temazepam use UGT glucuronidation only (Smolders et al., Clin Pharmacokinet 2016; Gronich, Drugs Aging 2024; Prince et al., Drugs 2023). Do not imply identical half-lives or metabolite profiles.

Explanation: These barbiturates enhance GABA-A-mediated inhibition, classically by increasing the duration of chloride-channel opening (contrast with benzodiazepines, which increase opening frequency).
Source Section: Substance Misuse / Barbiturates; PDF p. 62
Notes: All four are barbiturates; duration-vs-frequency mechanism is standard pharmacology (no primary trial reference retrieved). Clinical uses differ (phenobarbital anticonvulsant, thiopental/pentobarbital anesthetic-sedative); do not imply interchangeable indications. Selected four of a larger class.

Explanation: These analgesics exert clinically important full agonist activity at the mu-opioid receptor.
Source Section: Substance Misuse / Opioid Classification; PDF p. 60
Notes: Confirmed as full mu agonists (Roberts et al., Nat Rev Dis Primers 2026 toxidrome table; Harris et al., JAMA 2026). Do not imply identical kinetics/safety; methadone adds NMDA antagonism and QT prolongation. Distinguish from partial agonist (buprenorphine) and antagonists.

Explanation: These are high-potency first-generation (typical) antipsychotics with strong D2 blockade and correspondingly high extrapyramidal-symptom risk.
Source Section: Psychiatric Pharmacology / Typical Antipsychotics; PDF p. 86
Notes: Membership and high EPS risk are standard. Reject the source claim that D2 blockade 'augments dopamine signaling' or that 'dopamine antagonizes prolactin receptors'—D2 blockade reduces dopamine signaling and raises prolactin by disinhibition. Shared high EPS risk is a board-overlap consideration.

Explanation: These four movement disorders occur with dopamine-receptor-blocking antipsychotics and differ in manifestations and usual onset.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Antipsychotic EPS syndromes; Extrapyramidal side effects
Source Section: Psychiatric Pharmacology / Extrapyramidal Effects; PDF p. 88
Notes: Four classic EPS confirmed (Chun et al., AAP 2016; Pereira & Albert, Cochrane 2017; Marder & Cannon, NEJM 2019). NMS is correctly excluded (it is a systemic hyperthermic emergency, not a discrete movement disorder). Do not use the '3-hour/3-day/3-week/3-year' mnemonic as diagnostic cutoffs.

Explanation: An acute dystonic reaction can cause sustained abnormal contraction of neck, facial, ocular (oculogyric crisis), or laryngeal muscles after dopamine-blocking drug exposure.
Source Section: Psychiatric Pharmacology / Extrapyramidal Effects; PDF p. 88
Notes: Oculogyric crisis, laryngeal dystonia, and neck/facial involvement confirmed (Chun et al., AAP 2016). These are possible, not obligatory, manifestations; laryngeal spasm is the life-threatening form (airway emergency).

Explanation: Lithium impairs renal concentrating ability (nephrogenic DI), can cause hypothyroidism and fine tremor as patient adverse effects; prenatal exposure carries a classic association with Ebstein anomaly.
Source Section: Psychiatric Pharmacology / Lithium; PDF p. 85
Notes: Nephrogenic DI, hypothyroidism, tremor confirmed as patient adverse effects (McKnight et al., Cochrane 2019; Price & Heninger, NEJM 1994; FDA lithium label). Ebstein anomaly is a teratogenic/prenatal-exposure association (~1:1000)—a different exposure context; the mixed category is a fairness caveat. Do not imply an inevitable fetal outcome.

Explanation: These non-antidepressant agents can contribute to serotonin toxicity via distinct mechanisms (linezolid MAO inhibition; tramadol and meperidine serotonin reuptake inhibition; MDMA serotonin release), especially with other serotonergic exposures.
Source Section: Psychiatric Pharmacology / Serotonin Syndrome; PDF p. 89
Notes: Confirmed (Werneke et al., BMC Neurol 2016; Roberts et al., Nat Rev Dis Primers 2026; Chun et al., AAP 2016; tramadol FDA label). Association does not mean toxicity occurs with every exposure—risk is highest with combinations/overdose. Do not copy the simplified MDMA receptor mechanism from the source.

Explanation: NMS classically combines hyperthermia, marked (lead-pipe) rigidity, altered mental status, and autonomic instability after dopamine blockade.
Source Section: Psychiatric Pharmacology / Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome; PDF pp. 88-89
Notes: Tetrad confirmed (Suekane et al., Acta Psychiatr Scand 2026; APA Resource Document on Catatonia 2025). Board overlap: fever, altered mental status, and autonomic instability also occur in serotonin syndrome—lead-pipe rigidity (vs clonus/hyperreflexia) is the differentiating tile. Not sufficient alone for diagnosis.

Connection Title: Non-drug delirium reorientation and sleep measures
Explanation: Orientation cues (clocks, calendars), reduced nighttime disruption, and contact with familiar people are supportive non-pharmacologic measures for delirium.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Delirium orientation and sleep support; Non-pharmacologic delirium measures
Source Section: Memory, Dissociation, and Orientation / Delirium; PDF p. 23
Notes: Standard non-pharmacologic delirium reorientation/sleep-hygiene bundle; supportive only and does not replace identifying/treating the underlying cause. Limited direct primary reference retrieved; consistent with general delirium guidance. Clocks and calendars are intentionally separate source-listed cues (distinct tiles).
